content: Pediatric flat feet are a common condition encountered in primary care, with an estimated prevalence of approximately 15%. While most cases are asymptomatic, a minority of children with flat feet may experience pain and limitations in gait. Currently, there is no consensus or optimal strategy for the use of foot orthoses (FOs) in the treatment of pediatric flat feet. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of foot orthoses in managing pediatric flat feet. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed outcomes such as pain, function, quality of life (QoL), treatment success, and adverse events. Comparisons were made between custom foot orthoses (CFOs) and prefabricated foot orthoses (PFOs), as well as between FOs and regular shoes. A total of 16 trials involving 1,058 children aged 11 months to 19 years with flexible flat feet were included. The studies addressed various presentations of flat feet, including asymptomatic cases, symptomatic cases associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), and cases linked to developmental coordination disorder (DCD). Interventions included FOs, footwear, foot exercises, rehabilitative exercises, and neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES). Due to significant heterogeneity among the studies, data pooling was not performed. Most trials were at risk of bias due to issues such as lack of blinding and selective reporting. For asymptomatic flat feet in healthy children, the evidence was of low to very low certainty. One trial comparing CFOs to shoes (106 participants) found little to no difference in pain reduction (measured on a 10-point visual analogue scale) or adverse event withdrawals after one year. Similarly, a trial comparing PFOs to shoes (106 participants) showed no significant differences in pain or adverse events. When CFOs were compared to PFOs (108 participants), no differences were observed in pain outcomes or adverse event withdrawals. Function and quality of life were not assessed in these trials. For symptomatic flat feet associated with JIA, the evidence was also of low to very low certainty. One trial (28 participants) comparing CFOs to shoes over a 3-month follow-up period showed minimal differences in pain reduction but suggested improvements in function (measured by the Foot Function Index) and QoL (measured by the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory, PedsQL). Another trial (25 participants) comparing PFOs to shoes found no significant differences in pain, function, or QoL. When CFOs were compared to PFOs (87 participants across two trials), no meaningful differences were observed in pain, function, or QoL outcomes. The authors concluded that the evidence supporting the use of CFOs or PFOs for pediatric flat feet is of low to very low certainty. The findings suggest that CFOs, which are more expensive, offer no clear advantage over PFOs or regular shoes in managing pain, function, or QoL in children with asymptomatic flat feet. For children with JIA, FOs may provide some benefit in terms of pain and function, but the differences between CFOs and PFOs remain minimal. The review highlights the lack of evidence to justify the use of high-cost CFOs for healthy children with flexible flat feet in the absence of pain. It emphasizes the need to shift research focus away from asymptomatic flat feet in healthy children and toward conditions that cause pain, limit function, or reduce QoL, such as JIA, cerebral palsy, congenital talipes equinovarus, trisomy 21, and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Future research should prioritize these clinically significant pediatric foot conditions rather than continuing to investigate asymptomatic flat feet in healthy children.
